\chapter{Methodology}

\section{The Zero-Score Expectation Parameter}

@severini2007 considered the problem of selecting a weight function $\pi(\lambda|\psi)$ such that when the likelihood function is integrated with respect to this density over the nuisance parameter space, the result is useful for non-Bayesian inference. To do this, he outlined four properties (see Appendix \ref{appendix:B}) that an integrated likelihood must satisfy if it is to be of any use and went on to show that such a function could be obtained by doing the following:
\begin{enumerate}[label = \arabic*)]
  \item Find a reparameterization $(\psi, \lambda) \mapsto (\psi, \phi)$ of the model such that the new nuisance parameter $\phi$ is unrelated to $\psi$ in the sense that $\hat{\phi}_{\psi} = \hat{\phi}$; that is, the conditional maximum likelihood estimate of $\phi$ given $\psi$ is simply equal to the unrestricted maximum likelihood estimate of $\phi$.
  \item Select a prior density $\pi(\lambda|\psi)$ such that when the model undergoes the above reparameterization, the resulting prior density $\pi(\phi)$ does not depend on $\psi$.
\end{enumerate}
An integrated likelihood function for $\psi$ that possesses the desired properties will then be given by $$\bar{L}(\psi) = \int_{\Phi} \tilde{L}(\psi, \phi) \pi(\phi) d\phi,$${#eq-ZSE_IL1} where $\tilde{L}(\psi, \phi)$ is the likelihood function for the model after it has been reparameterized in terms of $\phi$. The exact choice of prior density for $\phi$ is not particularly important; the only restriction placed upon it is that it must not depend on $\psi$. Hence, the crux of the matter really lies in completing the first step. The approach taken by @severini2007 is to define a new nuisance parameter $\phi$ as the solution to the equation $$\text{E}_{(\psi_0, \lambda_0)}\Big[\nabla_{\lambda}\ell(\psi, \lambda; \mathbf{X}_n)\Big]\Bigg|_{(\psi_0, \lambda_0) = (\hat{\psi}, \phi)} = \mathbf{0},$${#eq-ZSE_IL2} where $\psi_0$ and $\lambda_0$ denote the true values of $\psi$ and $\lambda$, and $\hat{\psi}$ is the unrestricted MLE for $\psi_0$. The expectation here is being taken with respect to the data $\mathbf{X}_n = \mathbf{x}_n$ and not the parameters themselves. @eq-ZSE_IL2 can thus be rewritten as $$I(\psi, \lambda, \hat{\psi}, \phi) = \mathbf{0},$$ where $$I(\psi, \lambda, \psi_0, \lambda_0) = \int_{\mathbbm{R}^n} \big[\nabla_{\lambda}\ell(\psi, \lambda; \mathbf{x}_n)\big] p(\mathbf{x}_n; \psi_0, \lambda_0))d\mathbf{x}_n.$$

Assuming $I$ is invertible, for a particular value of $(\psi, \lambda, \hat{\psi})$, there will be a unique value of $\phi$ that solves @eq-ZSE_IL2. $\phi$ is called the *zero-score expectation* (ZSE) parameter because it is defined as the value that makes the expectation of the score function (in terms of $\lambda$, not the full parameter) with respect to $p(\mathbf{x}_n; \psi_0, \lambda_0)$ evaluated at the point $(\psi_0, \lambda_0) = (\hat{\psi}, \phi)$ equal to zero. This means that $\phi$ is really a function of $(\psi, \lambda, \hat{\psi})$, i.e., $\phi = \phi(\psi, \lambda, \hat{\psi})$. This in turn implies that $\phi$ is a function of the data through $\hat{\psi}$. Normally we try to avoid creating such dependencies in our parameters as it renders them useless for the purpose of parameterizing a statistical model. However, from the perspective of the likelihood function, once the data have been collected they are considered fixed in place and there is no issue with using a quantity such as $\phi$ that depends on the data to parameterize it.

For a given value of $\phi$, the corresponding value of $\lambda$ can be found by $$\lambda(\psi, \phi) = \underset{\lambda \in \Lambda}{\mathrm{argmax}} \> \text{E}_{(\hat{\psi}, \phi)}\big[\ell(\psi, \lambda; \mathbf{X}_n)\big].$${#eq-ZSE_IL3} For a certain choice of prior density $\pi(\phi)$, this allows us to write @eq-ZSE_IL1 in terms of $L(\psi, \lambda)$: $$\bar{L}(\psi) = \int_{\Phi} L(\psi, \lambda(\psi, \phi)) \pi(\phi) d\phi.$${#eq-ZSE_IL4} 

\section{Explicit Parameters of Interest}

\section{Implicit Parameters of Interest}

The procedure described in the previous section is based on the assumption that $\lambda$ is an explicit nuisance parameter so that taking partial derivatives of $\ell$ with respect to its components is a well-defined operation. However, @severini2018 proved that reparameterizing the model in terms of the ZSE parameter yields the same nice properties in the subsequent integrated likelihood when $\psi$ and $\lambda$ are implicit as well. In this section, we consider an approach to approximating the integrated likelihood function that has been adapted from this method.

Consider a model with parameter $\theta \in \Theta$ and implicit parameter of interest $\psi = \varphi(\theta)$ for some function $\varphi: \Theta \to \mathbbm{R}$. @eq-ZSE_IL4 tells us that we can calculate the integrated likelihood for $\psi$ if we know the value of $\theta$ corresponding to a given value of the ZSE parameter, and this will be true for models with both explicit and implict parameters. Let $\hat{\psi} = \varphi(\hat{\theta})$ denote the unrestricted MLE for $\psi$ and define the set $$\Omega_{\psi} = \Big\{\omega \in \Theta: \varphi(\omega) = \psi\Big\}.$${#eq-ZSE_IL6} Then an element of $\Omega_{\hat{\psi}}$ for a model without an explicit nuisance parameter is functionally equivalent to a value $(\hat{\psi}, \phi)$ for a model with an explicit nuisance parameter.

Generalizing the result in @eq-ZSE_IL3, for a given element $\omega \in \Omega_{\hat{\psi}}$, the corresponding value of $\theta$ is that which maximizes $\text{E}_{\omega}\big[\ell(\theta; \mathbf{X}_n)\big]$ subject to the restriction that $\varphi(\theta) = \psi$. This allows us to define a function $T_{\psi}: \Omega_{\hat{\psi}} \to \Theta(\psi)$ such that $T_{\psi}(\omega) = \underset{\theta \in \Theta(\psi)}{\mathrm{argmax}} \> \text{E}_{\omega}\big[\ell(\theta; \mathbf{X}_n)\big]$. The integrated likelihood for $\psi$ is then given by $$\bar{L}(\psi) = \int_{\Omega_{\hat{\psi}}} L\big(T_{\psi}(\omega)\big)\pi(\omega)d\omega,$${#eq-ZSE_IL7} where $\pi(\omega)$ is a density defined on $\Omega_{\hat{\psi}}$.

@eq-ZSE_IL7 can also be written as $$\bar{L}(\psi) = \text{E}_{\omega}\Big[L\big(T_{\psi}(W)\big)\Big],$${#eq-ZSE_IL8} where $W$ represents a random variable with density $\pi(\omega)$. We can further define a function $Q: \mathcal{U} \to \Omega_{\hat{\psi}}$ for some set $\mathcal{U}$ such that if $U$ is a random variable taking values in $\mathcal{U}$, then $Q(U)$ will be a random variable in $\Omega_{\hat{\psi}}$ with a distribution that is completely determined by our choice of $U$. Therefore, $$\bar{L}(\psi) = \text{E}_{\omega}\Big[L\big(T_{\psi}(Q(U))\big)\Big]$${#eq-ZSE_IL8} is an integrated likelihood for $\psi$ with a weight function corresponding to the density of $Q(U)$. 

Define $$\tilde{L}(u; \psi) = L(T_{\psi}(Q(u)), \> u \in \mathcal{U}.$${#eq-ZSE_IL9} Then we simply have $\overset{\sim}{L}(u; \psi) = L(\symbf{\theta})$, with $\symbf{\theta}$ taken to be $T_{\psi}(Q(u))$. $\overset{\sim}{L}(u; \psi)$ will be a genuine likelihood for the parameter $(u, \psi)$ provided that there always exists a value $(u, \psi)$ such that $T_{\psi}(Q(u)) = \symbf{\theta}_0$ for any possible value of $\symbf{\theta}_0$. A sufficient condition for this to occur is that for any $\psi \in \Psi$, $T_{\psi}(Q(\mathcal{U})) = \Omega_{\psi}$.

We can then write the integrated likelihood for $\psi$ in terms of $\overset{\sim}{L}(u; \psi)$ as follows: $$\bar{L}(\psi) = \int_{\mathcal{U}} \tilde{L}(u; \psi)\check{\pi}(u)du,$${#eq-ZSE_IL10} where $\check{\pi}(u)$ is a density on $\mathcal{U}$ of our choosing. If $\check{\pi}(u)$ doesn't depend on $\psi$, the integrated likelihood given by @eq-ZSE_IL10 will have the properties we desire.

We can further rewrite @eq-ZSE_IL10 as $$\bar{L}(\psi) = \int_{\Theta} \frac{\tilde{L}(u; \psi)}{\check{L}(u)} \check{L}(u)\check{\pi}(u)du,$${#eq-ZSE_IL11} where $\check{L}(u)$ represents an arbitrary likelihood function for the "parameter" $u$. From a Bayesian point of view, the quantity $\check{L}(u)\check{\pi}(u)$ can then be thought of as a posterior density for $u$ up to some proportionality constant. If $\check{\pi}(u)$ is chosen to be a conjugate prior for $\check{L}(u)$ such that the posterior density $\check{L}(u)\check{\pi}(u)$ has the same form as $\check{L}$ itself, and $\check{L}$ is chosen to be a known distribution, then random samples can be drawn directly from this posterior density using modern statistical computing packages. Alternatively, it may also be possible to obtain random samples from the posterior density through Monte Carlo methods such as importance sampling or MCMC.  

In either case, once random variates $u_1, ..., u_R$ have been sampled from $\check{L}(u)\check{\pi}(u)$, a simple empirical estimate to $\bar{L}(\psi)$ at a particular value of $\psi$ is given by $$\hat{\bar{L}}(\psi) = \frac{1}{R} \sum_{i = 1}^R \frac{\tilde{L}(u_i; \psi)}{\check{L}(u_i)}.$${#eq-ZSE_IL12} Repeating this procedure for every value of $\psi \in \Psi$ will give an overall shape for $\hat{\bar{L}}(\psi)$, which can be used to conduct inference for $\psi_0$ without interference from a nuisance parameter.

\section{Monte Carlo Approximation of the Integrated Likelihood}

\subsection{Omega-Hat Sampling and Branch-Mode Construction}

\subsubsection{Overview}

Integrated likelihood inference in this work proceeds by marginalizing
over nuisance configurations that are compatible with a fixed value of
the parameter of interest. In models where the nuisance parameter is
high-dimensional and subject to nonlinear constraints, direct
integration is infeasible. Instead, the \textit{likelyr} framework
approximates the integrated likelihood using a Monte Carlo--style
construction based on a collection of constrained profile likelihood
branches.

Each branch corresponds to a particular realization of an auxiliary
nuisance configuration, denoted $\hat{\omega}$, which satisfies a
defining constraint on the parameter of interest. The quality of the
integrated likelihood approximation therefore depends critically on (i)
how these $\hat{\omega}$ values are generated and (ii) how the
corresponding profile likelihood branches are constructed.

\subsubsection{Definition of $\hat{\omega}$}

Let $\theta \in \Theta \subset \mathbb{R}^d$ denote the full parameter
vector of the model, and let $\psi = g(\theta)$ be the scalar parameter
of interest. The maximum likelihood estimate of $\psi$ is denoted
$\hat{\psi}$.

An \textit{omega-hat} value, $\hat{\omega}$, is defined as a point in
the parameter space $\Theta$ satisfying
\begin{equation}
    g(\hat{\omega}) = \hat{\psi},
\end{equation}
along with any equality, inequality, or bound constraints imposed by the
model specification. Importantly, $\hat{\omega}$ is \textbf{not}
required to maximize the likelihood. Instead, it represents a feasible
nuisance configuration consistent with the observed estimate of the
parameter of interest.

The collection of all such $\hat{\omega}$ values forms a constrained
manifold in parameter space. Integrated likelihood inference proceeds by
averaging, in an approximate sense, over likelihood contributions
associated with different points on this manifold.

\subsubsection{The Role of the Parameter Space: Two Structural Cases}

A key distinction in the implementation of this framework concerns
whether $\hat{\omega}$ and the model parameter $\theta$ inhabit the
same space. This distinction has substantial consequences for both the
computational structure and the statistical interpretation of the
resulting integrated likelihood.

\paragraph{Case 1: $\hat{\omega}$ and $\theta$ share the same space.}
In the simplest setting---exemplified by the baseline multinomial model
with parameter $\theta \in \Delta^{J-1}$---the model parameter is
itself a probability vector, and the constraint set $\{g(\theta) =
\hat{\psi}\}$ is a manifold within the same ambient space. In this
case, $\hat{\omega}$ is drawn directly from $\Omega_{\hat{\psi}} =
\{\omega \in \Delta^{J-1} : g(\omega) = \hat{\psi}\}$, and the expected
log-likelihood is
\begin{equation}
    \mathbb{E}_{\hat{\omega}}[\ell(\theta)] =
    n \sum_{j=1}^J \hat{\omega}_j \log \theta_j,
\end{equation}
which is straightforwardly maximized subject to $g(\theta) = \psi$ by a
constrained optimization over $\theta \in \Delta^{J-1}$.

Because $\hat{\omega}$ and $\theta$ are the same type of object, the
unconstrained maximizer of $\mathbb{E}_{\hat{\omega}}[\ell(\theta)]$
over $\theta$ is precisely $\hat{\omega}$ itself, by the information
inequality. It follows that at $\psi = \hat{\psi}$, the constrained
maximizer of the expected log-likelihood is $\hat{\omega}$, and when
$\hat{\omega} = \hat{\theta}$ (the MLE), the branch evaluated at
$\hat{\psi}$ returns $\ell(\hat{\theta})$---the unconstrained maximum
of the observed log-likelihood. The profile likelihood therefore
achieves its maximum exactly at $\hat{\psi}$, and the surrogate
objective is fully aligned with the true log-likelihood at the reference
point.

\paragraph{Case 2: $\hat{\omega}$ and $\theta$ inhabit different spaces.}
In regression settings---such as the multinomial logistic regression
model considered in this work---the model parameter is a matrix of
regression coefficients $B \in \mathbb{R}^{p \times (J-1)}$, while the
parameter of interest is the Simpson's index of the conditional
probability vector at a reference covariate value $\mathbf{x}_0$:
\begin{equation}
    \psi(B) = D\!\left(\boldsymbol{\theta}(\mathbf{x}_0; B)\right)
    = \sum_{j=1}^J \theta_j(\mathbf{x}_0; B)^2.
\end{equation}
Here $\boldsymbol{\theta}(\mathbf{x}_0; B) = \mathrm{softmax}(B^\top
\mathbf{x}_0) \in \Delta^{J-1}$, so the level set
$\Omega_{\hat{\psi}}$ is a manifold in $\Delta^{J-1}$, whereas the
model parameter lives in $\mathbb{R}^{p(J-1)}$. These two spaces have
different dimension and different geometric structure.

To bridge this gap, $\hat{\omega}$ is sampled as a probability vector
from the sphere $\Omega_{\hat{\psi}} \subset \Delta^{J-1}$, and the
corresponding model parameter is recovered via a rank-1 adjustment of
the MLE. Specifically, given $\hat{\omega} \in \Omega_{\hat{\psi}}$,
define
\begin{equation}
    \hat{B}(\hat{\omega}) = \hat{B}_{\mathrm{MLE}} +
    \frac{\mathbf{x}_0
    \bigl(\boldsymbol{\eta}_0 - \hat{B}_{\mathrm{MLE}}^\top
    \mathbf{x}_0\bigr)^\top}{\|\mathbf{x}_0\|^2},
\end{equation}
where $\boldsymbol{\eta}_0 = \log(\hat{\omega}_{-J}) -
\log(\hat{\omega}_J)$ is the logit vector corresponding to $\hat{\omega}$
at the reference point. This construction satisfies
$\boldsymbol{\theta}(\mathbf{x}_0; \hat{B}(\hat{\omega})) = \hat{\omega}$
exactly, while leaving the regression coefficients unchanged in all
directions orthogonal to $\mathbf{x}_0$. The expected log-likelihood
used as the branch objective is then
\begin{equation}
    \mathbb{E}_{\hat{\omega}}[\ell(B)] = \sum_{i=1}^n
    \boldsymbol{\theta}(\mathbf{x}_i; \hat{B}(\hat{\omega}))^\top
    \boldsymbol{\eta}(\mathbf{x}_i; B) -
    \sum_{i=1}^n \log Z(\mathbf{x}_i; B),
\end{equation}
where $\boldsymbol{\theta}(\mathbf{x}_i; \hat{B}(\hat{\omega}))$ are
the observation-specific reference probabilities induced by
$\hat{\omega}$ through $\hat{B}$, and $Z(\mathbf{x}_i; B)$ is the
partition function at covariate $\mathbf{x}_i$.

This dimension mismatch has an important statistical consequence. In
Case 1, the surrogate objective $\mathbb{E}_{\hat{\omega}}[\ell(\theta)]$
and the observed log-likelihood $\ell(\theta)$ are globally aligned: the
unconstrained maximizer of the surrogate is $\hat{\omega}$, which at
$\hat{\omega} = \hat{\theta}$ is also the unconstrained MLE. In Case 2,
this alignment breaks down. The unconstrained maximizer of
$\mathbb{E}_{\hat{\omega}}[\ell(B)]$ is $\hat{B}(\hat{\omega})$---not
$\hat{B}_{\mathrm{MLE}}$---because $\hat{B}(\hat{\omega})$ is
constructed to satisfy $\boldsymbol{\theta}(\mathbf{x}_0; \cdot) =
\hat{\omega}$, which generally differs from the MLE in directions other
than $\mathbf{x}_0$. As a result, $\ell(\hat{B}(\hat{\omega}_{\mathrm{MLE}}))
\neq \ell(\hat{B}_{\mathrm{MLE}})$ in general, and the approximate
profile likelihood---defined as $\ell(\hat{\theta}(\psi;
\hat{\omega}_{\mathrm{MLE}}))$ where $\hat{\omega}_{\mathrm{MLE}} =
\boldsymbol{\theta}(\mathbf{x}_0; \hat{B}_{\mathrm{MLE}})$---need not
achieve its maximum exactly at $\hat{\psi}$.

This drift is a direct consequence of working with a conditional
parameter of interest in a regression model: the natural sampling space
for $\hat{\omega}$ (probability vectors in $\Delta^{J-1}$) differs from
the model parameter space ($\mathbb{R}^{p(J-1)}$), and the rank-1
construction that bridges them introduces a gap between the surrogate
and true objectives. In well-specified models with moderate sample
sizes, this gap is small and the resulting shift in the profile maximum
is negligible. It is, however, a structural feature of the framework in
this setting and not a numerical artifact.

\subsubsection{Rationale for Sampling $\hat{\omega}$}

In many applications, the constraint $g(\theta) = \hat{\psi}$ does not
uniquely determine $\theta$. The set of feasible $\hat{\omega}$ values
may be high-dimensional, nonconvex, and possess nontrivial symmetries.
No single $\hat{\omega}$ can therefore be regarded as representative of
the nuisance uncertainty.

Rather than attempting to enumerate or integrate over this constraint
set directly, \textit{likelyr} samples a finite collection of
$\hat{\omega}$ values and constructs a corresponding collection of
profile likelihood branches, which are later combined to approximate the
integrated likelihood. The role of the $\hat{\omega}$ sampling scheme is
twofold:
\begin{enumerate}
    \item \textbf{Exploration}: to cover different regions of the
    constraint set $\{g(\theta) = \hat{\psi}\}$, including
    symmetry-related configurations.
    \item \textbf{Stability}: to preferentially select nuisance
    configurations that lead to well-behaved profile likelihood branches.
\end{enumerate}
These objectives are in tension: overly aggressive exploration can lead
to nuisance configurations that induce unstable or degenerate branches,
while overly conservative sampling can fail to capture important
variation in the nuisance structure.

\subsubsection{Generating Candidate $\hat{\omega}$ Values}

The sampling of $\hat{\omega}$ proceeds in two stages: generation of an
initial guess, followed by projection onto the constraint set.

\paragraph{Initial Guess Generation.}
The initial guess generator produces candidate parameter vectors in the
ambient space $\Theta$. These candidates are not required to satisfy the
constraint $g(\theta) = \hat{\psi}$, but are intended to lie in regions
of parameter space plausibly relevant for integrated likelihood
inference. The generator typically combines recentering around the
full-model MLE $\hat{\theta}$, perturbations within the tangent space of
the constraint manifold at $\hat{\theta}$, and occasional global or
symmetry-driven moves. The specific form is treated as a
user-configurable component of the nuisance specification, allowing
problem-specific structure to be encoded where available.

\paragraph{Projection to a Feasible $\hat{\omega}$.}
Given an initial guess, the algorithm computes a corresponding
$\hat{\omega}$ by solving a constrained feasibility problem:
\begin{equation}
    \text{find } \hat{\omega} \quad \text{such that} \quad
    g(\hat{\omega}) = \hat{\psi},
\end{equation}
along with any additional model constraints. This step does not optimize
the likelihood; it projects the initial guess onto the constraint set
using an augmented Lagrangian solver. Repeating this procedure yields a
collection $\{\hat{\omega}^{(1)}, \ldots, \hat{\omega}^{(R)}\}$ of
feasible nuisance configurations.

In Case 1, this projection step directly produces a draw from
$\Omega_{\hat{\psi}} \subset \Theta$. In Case 2, it produces a draw
from the corresponding sphere in $\Delta^{J-1}$, from which a
coefficient matrix is recovered via the rank-1 construction described
above.

\subsubsection{From $\hat{\omega}$ to Branch Modes}

Each $\hat{\omega}$ induces a distinct constrained optimization problem
for the full parameter $\theta$. For fixed $\hat{\omega}$ and a given
value of $\psi$, the branch is defined by
\begin{equation} \label{eq:branch_evaluator}
    \hat{\theta}(\psi; \hat{\omega}) = \underset{g(\theta) = \psi}
    {\arg\max} \; \mathbb{E}_{\hat{\omega}}\bigl[\ell(\theta)\bigr],
\end{equation}
together with any additional constraints. The expected log-likelihood
$\mathbb{E}_{\hat{\omega}}[\ell(\theta)]$ plays the role of the
surrogate objective: rather than maximizing the observed log-likelihood
directly---which would collapse all branches onto the profile
likelihood---the algorithm maximizes the expectation of the
log-likelihood under the nuisance configuration encoded by $\hat{\omega}$.
This is precisely the construction of @severini2018, generalized
to the implicit-parameter setting via \eqref{eq-ZSE_IL7}.

A critical implementation detail concerns the optimization variable in
\eqref{eq:branch_evaluator}. In both cases, the quantity being
optimized is $\theta$---the full model parameter---not $\hat{\omega}$.
The role of $\hat{\omega}$ is solely to parametrize the surrogate
objective: it enters through $\mathbb{E}_{\hat{\omega}}[\cdot]$ and is
held fixed while the optimizer searches over $\theta$. In Case 1, where
$\hat{\omega}$ and $\theta$ share the same space, $\hat{\omega}$ itself
serves as a natural warm start for the optimizer. In Case 2, however,
$\hat{\omega}$ is a probability vector of dimension $J$ while $\theta =
\mathrm{vec}(B)$ has dimension $p(J-1)$; supplying $\hat{\omega}$ as a
warm start would produce a dimension mismatch. Instead, the algorithm
uses $\hat{\theta}_{\mathrm{MLE}}$ as the initial value for the
optimizer in Case 2, since it is always a valid element of the model
parameter space.

Before tracing an entire branch, the algorithm first locates the
\textbf{branch mode}, defined as
\begin{equation}
    \psi^{\ast}(\hat{\omega}) = \underset{\psi}{\arg\max} \;
    \ell\!\bigl(\hat{\theta}(\psi; \hat{\omega})\bigr).
\end{equation}
In practice, this is found via a golden section search over the
parameter of interest domain: a sequence of candidate $\psi$ values is
evaluated by solving \eqref{eq:branch_evaluator} at each, and the
$\psi$ that yields the highest observed log-likelihood is identified as
the mode. The branch mode serves as the anchor point for constructing
left and right profile likelihood branches and provides a natural
reference for assessing local curvature and branch regularity. Only
after a branch mode has been successfully located does the algorithm
proceed to trace the profile likelihood curve outward in both directions
from $\psi^{\ast}$.

Throughout the outward traversal, solutions are chained: the optimizer
at each grid point $\psi_k$ is initialized from $\hat{\theta}(\psi_{k-1};
\hat{\omega})$, the solution at the previous step. This warm-start
strategy exploits the continuity of $\hat{\theta}(\psi; \hat{\omega})$
in $\psi$ and reduces the risk of the optimizer converging to a
disconnected local optimum. As in the branch evaluation step, warm
starts must lie in the model parameter space $\Theta$, not in the
$\hat{\omega}$ space.

\subsubsection{Branch Aggregation and Regularization}

The integrated likelihood estimator implemented in \textit{likelyr}
implicitly relies on local quadratic approximations to the constrained
likelihood. Nuisance configurations that fail to induce a unimodal,
locally quadratic profile likelihood branch violate these assumptions
and are excluded from the Monte Carlo approximation. This truncation can
be interpreted as a regularization of the nuisance integration measure,
restricting attention to configurations for which the estimator is
well-defined and numerically stable. Empirically, such configurations
contribute negligibly in well-identified models, and their exclusion
substantially improves estimator stability.
